sections.title: Check which elements a hydrocarbon contains
paragraphs: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only. Check the entire formula, not whether it begins with C and H. Methane and ethene are hydrocarbons; ethanol contains oxygen and is not a hydrocarbon, although it is an organic compound.

A mixture of carbon and hydrogen elements is not automatically a hydrocarbon compound. Nor is every carbon-containing compound a hydrocarbon. This classification describes composition; it does not by itself tell you whether the molecule is saturated, branched or a gas.

example.question: Which of C₃H₈, C₂H₅OH and CH₃Cl are hydrocarbons?
steps: C₃H₈ contains only carbon and hydrogen and is a hydrocarbon.
C₂H₅OH contains oxygen; CH₃Cl contains chlorine.
The latter two are not hydrocarbons.
example.explanation: Every element in the formula matters.

commonMistakes: Calling every organic molecule a hydrocarbon.
Ignoring an oxygen or halogen at the end of a formula.

practice.question: Classify CH₄ and C₂H₅OH as hydrocarbons or non-hydrocarbons, giving the composition reason. Also classify C₆H₁₄, CH₃COOH and a mixture of separate carbon and hydrogen elements.
practice.answer: CH₄ is a hydrocarbon because it contains carbon and hydrogen only. C₂H₅OH is not a hydrocarbon because it also contains oxygen. C₆H₁₄ is a hydrocarbon; CH₃COOH is not because it includes oxygen; a physical mixture of separate C and H elements is not a hydrocarbon compound.
practice.explanation: Being an organic compound is not sufficient to make a substance a hydrocarbon. Check every element in its formula.

sections.title: Separate molecular, empirical, general and structural formulas
paragraphs: A molecular formula gives the actual atom counts in one molecule, such as C₄H₈. Its empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio, here CH₂. A general formula describes a family under stated conditions, such as CₙH₂ₙ for an acyclic hydrocarbon with one C=C bond; n is the number of carbon atoms.

A structural formula shows how atoms or groups connect: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ identifies but-1-ene, whereas C₄H₈ alone does not. A displayed formula shows every atom and every covalent bond, including C–H bonds and both lines of a C=C bond.

Check that each carbon has four bond contributions and each hydrogen one. Condensed CH₃ and CH₂ labels save space in structural formulas, but do not count as a fully displayed formula. Neither rotating a drawing nor grouping its letters differently changes the molecule’s connectivity.

example.question: For CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, give the molecular and empirical formulas and explain what its structural formula adds.
steps: Count four carbons and eight hydrogens: C₄H₈.
Divide both counts by four: CH₂.
The structural formula locates the double bond at one end of the connected four-carbon chain.
example.explanation: Atom counts and connectivity answer different questions.

commonMistakes: Using a general formula as the molecular formula of a specific molecule.
Calling CH₃CH₃ fully displayed.
Reducing a molecular formula when the question asks for actual atom counts.

practice.question: A molecule has molecular formula C₆H₁₂. Give its empirical formula and explain the reduction. Separately, for supplied pent-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃, give molecular, empirical and stated-family general formulas, then draw the fully displayed form and explain what its structural formula specifies.
practice.answer: CH₂. Divide both atom counts by their greatest common factor, 6, to give the simplest whole-number ratio 1:2. For pent-2-ene: C₅H₁₀, CH₂, and CₙH₂ₙ for the stated acyclic one-C=C family. Its structural formula fixes a five-carbon chain and the double bond between carbons2/3. In your displayed drawing show both C=C lines and every C–H bond: H counts along the chain are3,1,1,2,3, giving each carbon four bond contributions.
practice.explanation: The empirical formula describes a ratio. It does not mean the original molecule contains only one carbon atom and two hydrogen atoms.

sections.title: Recognize a homologous series, functional group and isomers
paragraphs: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical behaviour; successive members by carbon number differ by CH₂. Where a characteristic functional group defines the family, members share it. Physical properties such as boiling point generally vary gradually with increasing molecular size.

A functional group is the atom or group associated with characteristic reactions, such as the C=C group used for the alkene family in this syllabus. Do not confuse changing the carbon-chain length with changing the functional group.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connections between atoms. They are different compounds rather than successive homologous members, which differ in formula. Drawing the same connected chain backwards does not create a structural isomer.

example.question: Are ethene C₂H₄ and propene C₃H₆ structural isomers?
steps: Their molecular formulas differ by CH₂.
They are successive members of the alkene series.
They are not structural isomers because the molecular formulas are not the same.
example.explanation: Formula equality is essential to structural isomerism.

commonMistakes: Calling any two compounds with C=C isomers.
Calling a rotated drawing a different molecule.
Assuming similar chemical properties mean identical physical properties.

practice.question: Compare pentane C₅H₁₂ with hexane C₆H₁₄, and pentane with CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. Which pair are successive homologues and which are structural isomers? Name the alkene functional group and explain why sharing it does not make any two alkenes isomers.
practice.answer: Pentane/hexane are successive alkane homologues: their formulas differ by CH₂ and they have similar family chemistry. Pentane/CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ are structural isomers: both are C₅H₁₂ but their connections differ. The alkene group is C=C; sharing that group does not establish equal molecular formulas, which is also necessary for isomerism.
practice.explanation: A homologous series has a common general formula, similar chemical behaviour and a gradual physical-property trend. Same family is not the same compound; different chain length is not the same molecular formula.

sections.title: Use carbon counts and positions to read names
paragraphs: For the relevant simple chains, learn the first six carbon-count roots: meth- for one, eth- for two, prop- for three, but- for four, pent- for five and hex- for six. Methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane and hexane are the corresponding unbranched alkanes. The specification expects relevant names up to six carbons, while individual drawing requirements have their own smaller limits.

For a simple unbranched alkene, use -ene and number to give the C=C bond the lower position. CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene; CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is but-2-ene. The number names the first carbon of the double bond, not a count of double bonds.

For a simple branched alkane, choose the longest connected carbon chain as the parent and number it from the end giving the branch the lower position. In CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ the longest chain is five carbons, not six: its sixth carbon is a methyl branch, giving 2-methylpentane rather than 4-methylpentane. A straight-chain root and a total molecular carbon count are not always the same thing.

Alcohol names use the -ol ending, carboxylic acid names the -oic acid ending, and simple ester names join the alcohol-derived alkyl name with the acid-derived alkanoate name. The later drawing and ester-naming lessons show the required named sets and how to trace both parts. The general six-carbon scope does not turn a selected four-carbon drawing requirement into a completed whole-chapter audit.

Paper 2C naming extension: apply the same carbon roots to relevant alcohol and acid structures up to six carbons, counting the COOH carbon in an acid. For example, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH is pentan-1-ol and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂COOH is hexanoic acid. For an ester, count both acid- and alcohol-derived parts; the later ester task works in both directions within six total carbons. These extensions do not change the smaller specifically named drawing sets.

example.question: Name the unbranched structure CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂ using a lower double-bond position.
steps: Number from the CH₂ double-bond end.
The chain has four carbons and the double bond starts at carbon 1.
The name is but-1-ene, not but-3-ene.
example.explanation: Choose numbering from connectivity, not the left edge of the written formula.

commonMistakes: Counting a branch as part of a longer disconnected parent chain.
Calling the locant a number of double bonds.
Assuming all later naming scope is finished by learning six roots.

practice.question: Write the unbranched alkane names for one through six carbons. Name CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CH₂ and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃, explaining numbering and parent-chain length. Paper 2C extension: name CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂COOH.
practice.answer: Methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane, hexane. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CH₂ is pent-1-ene: number from the double-bond end. The branched structure is 2-methylpentane: the longest connected chain has five carbons and a methyl branch at the lower position 2, with six carbons in total. Paper 2C extension: pentan-1-ol and hexanoic acid; count the COOH carbon in the latter.
practice.explanation: The root describes the chosen parent chain, not necessarily every carbon in a branched molecule. The relevant naming scope reaches six carbons; the specific alkane/alkene drawing sets have smaller limits. The later alcohol/acid/ester topics are Paper 2C extensions.

sections.title: Generate different connections without duplicating rotations
paragraphs: To propose structural formulas from a molecular formula, choose a connected carbon framework, add any required functional group or unsaturation, and complete hydrogens to the normal valencies. Recount all atoms afterwards. A correct atom total with an impossible carbon valency is not a valid isomer.

For the acyclic saturated formula C₄H₁₀, a four-carbon chain gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃. A three-carbon chain with a methyl branch gives CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃. These are the two distinct connectivities. Reversing either drawing or bending its chain does not produce a third.

A molecular formula alone can leave the compound family ambiguous. For example, C₄H₈ can describe an acyclic alkene or a cyclic saturated hydrocarbon. Use the stated family and task scope rather than claiming a general formula uniquely proves a functional group; ring structures are not added to this introductory drawing bank.

example.question: Why is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ written from the other end not a new C₄H₁₀ isomer?
steps: It still connects the same four-carbon chain.
Only the orientation on the page changed.
A new structural isomer needs different atom connections.
example.explanation: Connectivity, not drawing direction, identifies the compound.

commonMistakes: Counting the same chain twice.
Giving a carbon five bond contributions.
Assuming CₙH₂ₙ alone proves an alkene.

practice.question: Draw both structural and fully displayed formulas for every acyclic alkane with formula C₄H₁₀. Give the unbranched name, check each carbon’s valency, and explain why reversing a drawing adds no isomer. Does C₄H₈ alone prove an alkene?
practice.answer: The two connections are CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butane) and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃. In the displayed straight chain the ends each have three H and the internal carbons two. In the branched structure the central carbon bonds to three carbons and one H; each outer carbon has three H. Both total C₄H₁₀ with four bond contributions per C. Reversal preserves connections. C₄H₈ alone does not prove an alkene; a cyclic structure can have that formula.
practice.explanation: Expand every C–H bond, using the original straight/branched drawing sheets to check your drawing. Same atom counts are necessary but not enough: different connections and valid valencies are required. The formula’s family conditions matter.

sections.title: Classify substitution, addition and combustion
paragraphs: In substitution, one atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another; an alkane hydrogen replaced by a halogen is the named example. In addition, groups add across a multiple bond, giving a product with no small molecule removed in the simple alkene example.

Combustion is reaction with oxygen that releases energy. Complete hydrocarbon combustion makes carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion can form carbon monoxide or carbon as well. Classify from the chemical change and products rather than the number of words in an equation.

The current alkane and alkene requirements do not require reaction mechanisms. Balance ordinary equations and retain the stated conditions without inventing radical or curly-arrow detail as a compulsory part of this course.

example.question: Classify a change in which each carbon of an ethene C=C gains a bromine atom to form one dibromoalkane.
steps: Bromine adds across the C=C bond.
The carbon-carbon bond becomes single.
This is addition, not replacement of a hydrogen.
example.explanation: Follow which bonds and atoms change.

commonMistakes: Calling addition substitution because bromine is a halogen.
Classifying from the number of products alone.

practice.question: Classify these supplied changes and justify from the atoms/bonds: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl under UV; CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Must you draw a reaction mechanism for these course examples?
practice.answer: The first is substitution: one H is replaced by Cl, with HCl formed. The second is addition: Br adds across C=C, which becomes C–C, without removing H. The third is complete combustion: methane reacts with oxygen, forming CO₂ and water and releasing energy. Reaction mechanisms are not required for these specified alkane/alkene examples.
practice.explanation: A halogen appearing in the reactants does not by itself distinguish addition from substitution. Follow the structural change and products, not just the number of products.

sections.title: Treat crude oil and its fractions as mixtures
paragraphs: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different molecular sizes and structures. It is not one compound with one molecular formula or one fixed boiling point. Its composition depends on the sample.

A fraction collects compounds with a similar range of boiling temperatures. It still contains more than one substance and is not a pure single alkane. Fractional distillation separates existing components by physical behaviour; it does not break the carbon chains as cracking does.

example.question: Does a collected gasoline fraction have to be one pure hydrocarbon?
steps: No: a fraction contains a range of hydrocarbons with similar boiling behaviour.
Its boiling range reflects that mixture.
Separation into a fraction does not imply a single molecular formula.
example.explanation: A fraction is a useful grouped mixture.

commonMistakes: Assigning crude oil one molecular formula.
Calling fractional distillation a chemical cracking reaction.

practice.question: A model refinery sample separates into several boiling ranges. A student writes one molecular formula for the entire original sample and calls each collected fraction a pure alkane. Correct both claims. Does this separation itself create shorter molecules?
practice.answer: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons and has no single molecular formula or one fixed boiling point. Each fraction is still a mixture containing hydrocarbons with similar boiling behaviour. Fractional distillation separates existing molecules; it does not itself break long chains into shorter ones.
practice.explanation: A boiling range and a useful fraction name do not establish single-compound purity. Cracking is a separate chemical conversion.

sections.title: Follow vaporization, rising vapours and condensation
paragraphs: In the industrial model, crude oil is heated so many components vaporize. The vapour mixture enters a fractionating column with a hot lower region and a cooler upper region. Different hydrocarbons condense at different heights according to their boiling behaviour.

Higher-boiling components condense in the hotter lower regions, while lower-boiling components rise farther before condensing; the lightest gases leave near the top. Very high-boiling residue remains near the bottom. The process uses repeated vaporization and condensation to separate boiling ranges.

A diagram needs the direction of the temperature gradient, the incoming hot mixture and the relative outlet positions. It does not require an invented exact temperature or carbon-count cutoff for every fraction. Real refinery cuts vary; the six required fraction names are the course reference.

example.question: Where would a lower-boiling fraction be collected relative to a higher-boiling fraction in this model?
steps: The column is cooler higher up.
Lower-boiling vapours travel farther before condensing.
They are collected higher than the higher-boiling fraction.
example.explanation: Condensation depends on the local temperature and boiling behaviour.

commonMistakes: Putting the hottest part at the top.
Saying all vapours condense at the same temperature.
Confusing an outlet’s height with a molecule’s density alone.

diagram.alt: Original schematic crude-oil column, hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, with the required refinery gases, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen in order, and their common uses.
diagram.caption: Relative order and temperature gradient only; no universal exact boiling cutoffs or single-compound purity are implied.

practice.question: Sketch the industrial fractionating-column model: show the hot feed, the temperature direction and three hypothetical fractions with boiling ranges A = 60–90 °C, B = 180–220 °C and C = 300–350 °C. Put their outlets in relative order and explain why. The ranges are invented, not prescribed refinery cutoffs.
practice.answer: Show heated feed entering the lower region, a hot bottom and cooler top. From higher to lower liquid outlets put A, B, C: the lower-boiling vapours travel farther up before condensing; higher-boiling material condenses lower in the hotter column. Some light gases can leave at the top and high-boiling residue remains low down.
practice.explanation: The drawing must use the temperature gradient and condensation, not chain-breaking or a density-only argument. Repeated vaporization/condensation separates boiling ranges; the invented numbers do not imply each fraction is a pure compound.

sections.title: Recall the six required fractions and their uses
paragraphs: From lighter to heavier fractions, the required names are refinery gases, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen. Gasoline is also called petrol. Use the course’s named set rather than substituting an additional refinery cut for one of these six.

Refinery gases are used for cooking and heating fuels; gasoline fuels car engines; kerosene is used as aircraft jet fuel; diesel fuels suitable road vehicles and other diesel engines. Fuel oil is used for large-scale heating and fuels such as those in some ships and power stations. Bitumen is used for road surfaces and roofing.

These are common uses, not a claim that every vehicle, ship or power station uses the same fuel. Connect a use to appropriate volatility or flow properties when requested, and keep a fraction’s name separate from a single compound’s name.

example.question: Identify the required fraction commonly associated with jet aircraft and the heavy residue used to surface roads.
steps: Kerosene is commonly used as jet fuel.
Bitumen is used in road surfacing.
The two uses involve fractions from very different regions of the column.
example.explanation: Recall the named fraction-use pairs.

commonMistakes: Calling bitumen gasoline.
Replacing fuel oil with an unrelated fraction name.
Treating a common use as universal for every engine.

practice.question: Name the six course fractions in order from lighter to heavier, then match each to a common use: road surfacing/roofing; car petrol engines; cooking/heating gas; jet aircraft; diesel engines; large-scale heating and some ships/power stations.
practice.answer: Refinery gases—cooking/heating; gasoline (petrol)—car petrol engines; kerosene—jet aircraft; diesel—diesel engines; fuel oil—large-scale heating and some ships/power stations; bitumen—road surfacing/roofing. That is the lighter-to-heavier course order.
practice.explanation: These are common uses of mixtures, not a universal claim about every vehicle or power station. Keep all six names rather than substituting a different refinery cut.

sections.title: Relate molecular size to boiling and flow trends
paragraphs: Across the main crude-oil fractions from lighter to heavier material, average hydrocarbon size increases. The school trends are higher boiling ranges, greater viscosity and generally darker appearance. Viscosity describes resistance to flow; it is different from density.

Larger hydrocarbon molecules generally have stronger intermolecular attractions, requiring more energy to separate them into the gas phase. Do not say the covalent carbon-carbon bonds must be broken simply to boil a hydrocarbon. Branching and composition can affect individual compounds, so use the broad fraction trend rather than an absolute rule for every isomer.

Refinery gases do not have liquid viscosity under ordinary gas conditions. Comparisons of flow for liquid fractions should use the same temperature; warming can change viscosity substantially. The general colour trend refers to the mixtures, not a claim that every long-chain pure alkane is dark.

example.question: Why does a heavier fraction usually need a higher temperature to boil?
steps: Its larger molecules generally attract one another more strongly.
More energy is needed to separate those molecules into vapour.
Boiling does not require breaking the covalent bonds within each molecule.
example.explanation: Distinguish intermolecular separation from chemical decomposition.

commonMistakes: Equating viscosity with density.
Saying longer carbon chains are broken during boiling.
Applying a mixture’s colour trend to every pure compound.

practice.question: Two unfamiliar liquid fractions are compared at the same temperature: L has smaller average hydrocarbon molecules and H larger ones. Give the expected broad trends in boiling range, viscosity and colour from L to H. Explain the boiling trend and identify two limits to this comparison.
practice.answer: From L to H, boiling range and viscosity generally increase and the mixtures generally become darker. Larger molecules usually have stronger intermolecular attractions, so separating them into vapour needs more energy; boiling does not require breaking their internal C–C bonds. These are broad mixture trends, not exact rankings for every isomer or a rule that every pure long-chain alkane is dark; viscosity depends on temperature.
practice.explanation: Viscosity is resistance to flow, not density. Compare liquid fractions at matched temperatures and do not assign a liquid-flow viscosity to refinery gases under ordinary gas conditions.

sections.title: Define a fuel by the energy released when burned
paragraphs: A fuel releases heat energy when it burns. Hydrocarbon fuels react with oxygen, transferring energy to the surroundings. A useful fuel choice may also depend on storage, availability, handling and unwanted emissions; these need supplied evidence rather than an invented universal ranking.

Ignition may be needed to overcome a barrier even though combustion is exothermic overall. Heat release is not the same as reaction rate or the fraction’s boiling point. A volatile fuel may be easier to ignite, but volatility alone does not establish a greater energy release per mole or gram.

example.question: Does needing an ignition spark mean gasoline combustion is endothermic overall?
steps: No: ignition can provide the initial activation input.
Combustion releases energy overall.
Starting a reaction and its net energy transfer are different questions.
example.explanation: Keep the initiation barrier separate from the overall change.

commonMistakes: Defining a fuel only as a liquid hydrocarbon.
Calling a high boiling point a measure of combustion energy.

practice.question: A hypothetical substance releases 12 kJ of heat overall when it burns after an ignition spark. Another substance simply evaporates at a low temperature. Which observation supports the definition of a fuel, and can the boiling behaviour alone rank combustion energy per gram?
practice.answer: The first substance satisfies the energy part of the fuel definition: burning releases heat overall. An ignition input does not make that net combustion endothermic. Low-temperature evaporation alone does not establish heat release on burning or a combustion-energy ranking per gram.
practice.explanation: Separate a physical boiling change, the activation input and the net chemical energy transfer. No claim about a real fuel’s safety, emissions or universal suitability follows from this invented comparison.

sections.title: Balance complete hydrocarbon combustion
paragraphs: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon with sufficient oxygen forms carbon dioxide and water. Carbon atoms set the number of CO₂ molecules, hydrogen atoms set the number of H₂O molecules, and the total product oxygen count sets the O₂ amount.

For propane, C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O conserves C₃, H₈ and O₁₀ on both sides. Do not change formula subscripts to balance an equation; adjust coefficients. Water may be vapour near the flame and condense after cooling.

A balanced equation describes the complete-combustion model, not a guarantee that any actual burner has sufficient oxygen. Exhaust samples can contain mixtures of products, unreacted gases and impurities.

example.question: Balance the complete combustion of C₄H₁₀ using whole-number coefficients.
steps: One C₄H₁₀ produces 4CO₂ and 5H₂O, requiring 6.5O₂.
Multiply through by two.
2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O.
example.explanation: Count carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen.

commonMistakes: Changing C₄H₁₀ to force an oxygen balance.
Omitting water from hydrocarbon combustion.
Assuming a balanced model proves complete real combustion.

practice.question: Balance complete combustion of ethane, C₂H₆, using the smallest whole-number coefficients. State the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen totals on each side. Does the balanced equation prove an actual burner has burned completely?
practice.answer: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Both sides contain C₄H₁₂O₁₄. Complete combustion forms carbon dioxide and water with sufficient oxygen, but the balanced model alone does not prove the conditions or products in an actual burner.
practice.explanation: Keep each substance’s formula unchanged and adjust coefficients. Water may be vapour near combustion and condense after cooling.

sections.title: Recognize carbon monoxide and soot as possible products
paragraphs: With insufficient oxygen or poor fuel-air mixing, hydrocarbon combustion can produce carbon monoxide, carbon particles and water, often together with some carbon dioxide. There is not one universal equation for every incomplete flame.

Illustrative limiting models include 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O and CH₄ + O₂ → C + 2H₂O. Both conserve atoms but describe different product choices. Carbon particles can appear as soot; carbon monoxide is not a visible black solid.

A sooty flame supports an incomplete-combustion concern, but absence of visible soot does not prove no carbon monoxide is present. These model equations do not replace appropriate combustion controls or gas measurements.

example.question: In the model 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O, check the atom totals.
steps: Left: C = 2, H = 8, O = 6.
Right: two CO supply C₂O₂ and four water supply H₈O₄.
The totals match; this is a CO-producing incomplete-combustion model.
example.explanation: A possible product equation still needs atom conservation.

commonMistakes: Calling soot carbon monoxide.
Giving only carbon dioxide as a possible incomplete product.
Using clear appearance as proof of no CO.

practice.question: Balance two possible incomplete-combustion models for propane: one forms only CO and water, the other carbon and water. Explain why neither is the single universal incomplete-combustion equation and why no visible soot is not proof of no CO.
practice.answer: CO model: 2C₃H₈ + 7O₂ → 6CO + 8H₂O, conserving C₆H₁₆O₁₄. Carbon model: C₃H₈ + 2O₂ → 3C + 4H₂O, conserving C₃H₈O₄. Real incomplete combustion can produce mixtures including CO, carbon, water and some CO₂, depending on oxygen supply and mixing. CO is a gas, not visible black soot, so absence of soot does not establish absence of CO.
practice.explanation: These are invented limiting product choices for balancing, not instructions to produce incomplete combustion. A model formula or appearance alone cannot certify combustion completeness.

sections.title: Explain carbon monoxide’s effect on oxygen transport
paragraphs: Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it reduces the blood’s capacity to transport oxygen. Less oxygen reaches body tissues for aerobic respiration. The required explanation focuses on that transport capacity; haemoglobin terminology is not required by this reference.

Do not explain the danger by saying CO is soot that blocks the lungs or that it simply uses up all the oxygen in a room. CO and CO₂ are different gases with different roles. This is the syllabus’s chemical and biological explanation, not a diagnosis or a detector reading.

example.question: Complete the explanation: carbon monoxide is dangerous because it reduces…
steps: …the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen.
That reduces oxygen delivery to tissues.
It is not explained by CO being a black solid.
example.explanation: Name the affected transport function.

commonMistakes: Confusing carbon monoxide with carbon dioxide.
Explaining the danger only by soot or irritation.

practice.question: Correct this explanation: “Carbon monoxide is black soot, and its danger is the same as carbon dioxide’s greenhouse effect.” Give the required blood-to-tissue chain without needing a protein name.
practice.answer: Carbon monoxide is a gas distinct from carbon soot and carbon dioxide. It reduces the blood’s capacity to transport oxygen, so less oxygen is delivered to tissues for aerobic respiration. This oxygen-transport effect is different from the greenhouse mechanism.
practice.explanation: The source requires the transport-capacity explanation; haemoglobin terminology is not required. This lesson does not diagnose an exposure or establish whether any environment is safe.

sections.title: Identify nitrogen and sulfur sources in combustion pollution
paragraphs: Air supplies nitrogen as well as oxygen. In a car engine, the high temperature can enable these gases to react and form oxides of nitrogen. Nitrogen need not have been part of the hydrocarbon molecule for nitrogen oxides to form.

Some fuels contain sulfur-bearing impurities. Their combustion can produce sulfur dioxide; the simple elemental-sulfur model is S + O₂ → SO₂. A pure hydrocarbon contains only C and H, so sulfur dioxide is not an unavoidable product from that pure formula alone.

Separate these sources: nitrogen oxides arise from high-temperature air chemistry in the named engine context, while sulfur dioxide can arise from fuel impurities. Cleaner sulfur content and altered combustion conditions address different contributors; no current emissions or policy figures are assumed.

example.question: Why can a sulfur-containing fuel mixture produce SO₂ even though a pure hydrocarbon has no sulfur?
steps: The fuel mixture can contain sulfur-bearing impurities.
Those impurities react with oxygen when burned.
The hydrocarbon-only formula does not describe every component of the fuel mixture.
example.explanation: Use the mixture composition rather than adding sulfur to an unrelated formula.

commonMistakes: Claiming sulfur is present in every pure alkane.
Claiming engine nitrogen oxides must come from nitrogen atoms in the fuel.

practice.question: A hypothetical engine burns a fuel mixture consisting mainly of hydrocarbons plus a small sulfur-bearing impurity, using air. Identify the separate sources and formation conditions for nitrogen oxides and SO₂. If sulfur impurities were removed, would that alone prevent nitrogen oxides?
practice.answer: High engine temperatures allow nitrogen and oxygen from air to react, forming nitrogen oxides. Sulfur-bearing fuel impurities can oxidise to SO₂; the simple sulfur model is S + O₂ → SO₂. Removing sulfur impurities addresses that sulfur source but does not alone prevent nitrogen/oxygen from air reacting at high temperature.
practice.explanation: A pure hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen; do not invent nitrogen or sulfur atoms in its formula to explain impurities or air-derived products. These are source mechanisms, not current emissions measurements.

sections.title: Connect sulfur and nitrogen oxides to acidic rain
paragraphs: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides can undergo reactions in the atmosphere and with water to form acidic substances that contribute to acid rain. The explanation needs the pollution gases, their conversion to acids and their incorporation into rainwater.

Do not describe these gases themselves as liquid acid falling from the exhaust. Several atmospheric reaction steps can be involved; a single simplified oxide-plus-water idea is not an exact model for every nitrogen oxide or every acid-rain sample.

Acid rain can harm organisms and react with susceptible materials such as carbonate stone. Carbon dioxide’s warming role is a different environmental pathway; avoid using “greenhouse gas” as the whole explanation for acid rain.

example.question: Improve “dirty fuel makes acid rain” into a chemical chain of explanation.
steps: Burning sulfur-containing impurities can release SO₂.
SO₂ undergoes atmospheric/water reactions that form acidic substances.
Those substances contribute to acidic rainwater.
example.explanation: Name the intermediate pollutant and its change, not only the outcome.

commonMistakes: Calling soot an acid gas.
Giving global warming as the acid-rain mechanism.

practice.question: An invented pollution report detects both SO₂ and nitrogen oxides. Explain how each can contribute to acidic rainwater and why “they trap heat, therefore the rain becomes acid” misses the chemical step. Is the exhaust itself necessarily liquid acid?
practice.answer: SO₂ and nitrogen oxides can undergo atmospheric reactions, including reactions involving water, that form acidic substances; those substances enter rainwater. Heat trapping is a different environmental pathway and does not supply the acid-formation explanation. The pollutant gases are not necessarily liquid acid leaving the exhaust.
practice.explanation: Several oxidation/water steps may be involved, so do not force every nitrogen oxide into one universal gas-plus-water equation. The lesson describes the chemical chain, not the exact composition of every rain sample.

sections.title: Use the specified catalytic cracking conditions
paragraphs: Catalytic cracking converts long-chain alkanes into shorter-chain alkanes and alkenes. In the specified model, use silica or alumina as the catalyst and a temperature in the range 600–700°C. Heating vaporized hydrocarbon over the hot catalyst changes chemical bonds rather than merely separating a mixture.

An original atom-balanced model is C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + 2C₂H₄. Carbon totals are 12 on both sides and hydrogen totals 26. This illustrates one possible product set, not a claim that a refinery produces only these compounds.

Cracking equations can have more than one valid product combination. Check every atom and whether the proposed saturated and unsaturated products fit the task. Other industrial processes can use different conditions; do not replace the own syllabus’s named catalytic conditions with a different cracking route.

example.question: For the model C₁₀H₂₂ → C₆H₁₄ + X, find X and identify its family if it is an acyclic molecule with one double bond.
steps: Subtract atoms: X has C₄H₈.
This fits CₙH₂ₙ with n = 4.
Under the supplied structure condition X is an alkene; the formula alone does not locate its double bond.
example.explanation: Conservation identifies a formula before structure is inferred.

commonMistakes: Calling fractional distillation cracking.
Ignoring a missing hydrogen in the product balance.
Giving an exact product identity without enough structural information.

practice.question: Complete the invented cracking model C₁₄H₃₀ → C₈H₁₈ + 2X. Give X’s formula, identify its family if each X is acyclic with one C=C bond, and state the own course’s catalytic conditions. Does this balance establish the only possible refinery products?
practice.answer: After subtracting C₈H₁₈, the two X molecules together contain C₆H₁₂, so each X is C₃H₆, an alkene under the stated structural condition. The model is C₁₄H₃₀ → C₈H₁₈ + 2C₃H₆, conserving C₁₄H₃₀. Use silica or alumina catalyst and 600–700 °C in the specified model. Other balanced product sets are possible; the equation does not establish a unique industrial product mixture.
practice.explanation: Long-chain alkane changes into shorter alkane and alkene products by chemical bond changes. Formula alone would not establish structure without the supplied acyclic/one-double-bond condition; this is not a home practical procedure.

sections.title: Explain why supply and demand motivate cracking
paragraphs: Crude oil supplies a particular distribution of fractions, while demand for useful products differs. A refinery may have more heavy long-chain material than demand requires and insufficient lighter fuels. Cracking converts some less-demanded long-chain material into more useful shorter products.

The shorter alkanes can contribute to fuel supply, and alkenes are useful starting materials for products such as polymers. Distillation alone cannot make more short molecules from long ones because it separates rather than changes the molecules.

Use any supplied production and demand data to identify the mismatch. The need is not that long-chain hydrocarbons contain no energy or can never be used; it is the balance between the available fractions and desired products.

example.question: A hypothetical refinery has excess heavy fractions but demand for more lighter fuel and alkene feedstock. Why does distillation alone not solve the mismatch?
steps: Distillation redistributes existing compounds into fractions.
It does not turn long molecules into shorter ones.
Cracking can change that molecular supply.
example.explanation: Connect the chemical process to the stated supply-demand problem.

commonMistakes: Saying heavy fractions are always useless.
Claiming separation creates new alkene molecules.

practice.question: Hypothetical supply/demand data, in equal mass units, are: heavy fraction supply 60, demand 35; lighter fuel supply 25, demand 40. Find each surplus/shortfall, explain why cracking can help and give a useful role for alkene products. Can the data alone tell exactly how much extra lighter fuel any chosen cracking process will make?
practice.answer: Heavy surplus = 60 − 35 = 25 units; lighter-fuel shortfall = 40 − 25 = 15 units. Cracking can convert some less-demanded long-chain material into shorter fuels and alkenes useful as feedstock, for example for polymers. Distillation alone only separates existing molecules. Exact lighter-fuel yield needs the actual cracking product distribution and conversion, which are not supplied.
practice.explanation: Supply/demand explains the need without claiming heavy fractions contain no energy or are always useless. Do not equate all cracked feed mass with one desired product.

sections.title: Use the alkane formula and explain saturation
paragraphs: Acyclic alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. With n = 5, the formula is C₅H₁₂. Saturated describes the absence of carbon-carbon multiple bonds: the carbon skeleton has single bonds and the normal hydrogen count for an acyclic alkane.

Saturation does not mean the sample is wet or that a solution cannot dissolve more solute. The term describes molecular bonding. A ring of saturated carbons has a different hydrogen-count formula, so apply CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ within the stated acyclic alkane family.
Branching does not change the molecular formula for a fixed number of carbons in an acyclic alkane. It changes connectivity and can change physical properties. Check formula and structure together.

example.question: An acyclic alkane has six carbons. Calculate its molecular formula.
steps: Hydrogens = 2 × 6 + 2 = 14.
The formula is C₆H₁₄; its particular connectivity still needs a structure.
example.explanation: A family formula gives atom counts under explicit conditions.

commonMistakes: Using CₙH₂ₙ for an acyclic alkane.
Confusing saturation with a saturated solution.

practice.question: An unfamiliar acyclic alkane has seven carbons. Give its molecular formula and explain saturation. Would branching change that formula, and does saturated mean unable to dissolve more solute?
practice.answer: C₇H₁₆, from H = 2(7) + 2. It is saturated because it has no carbon–carbon multiple bond; its carbon skeleton has single bonds. Branching changes connections but not this formula for seven carbons in the acyclic alkane family. Saturated solution is a different meaning of saturated.
practice.explanation: This applies the supplied general formula; naming or drawing every seven-carbon isomer is not required by the named small-molecule drawing set. Ring structures need a different formula condition.

sections.title: Draw the first five unbranched alkanes
paragraphs: The five unbranched examples are methane CH₄, ethane CH₃CH₃, propane CH₃CH₂CH₃, butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and pentane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. The condensed formulas show connectivity; a displayed answer must expand every C–H bond.

For a displayed acyclic alkane chain, draw single C–C bonds, give each terminal carbon three hydrogens and each internal unbranched carbon two. Methane is the one-carbon case with four hydrogens. Recount the atom totals and verify four bond contributions around every carbon.

The original drawing sheet is a two-dimensional bond representation, not the real bond angles or a claim that the molecules are flat. The required alkane drawing range is up to five carbons; the general naming reference extends to relevant compounds with six.

example.question: Draw fully displayed unbranched pentane and verify its hydrogens.
steps: Draw a connected five-carbon single-bond chain; expand three C–H bonds at each end and two at each of the three internal carbons, as shown on the drawing sheet.
Two terminal CH₃ groups contribute six H.
Three internal CH₂ groups contribute six H.
Total twelve H: C₅H₁₂.
example.explanation: Use connectivity and carbon valency to check the drawing.

commonMistakes: Giving a terminal carbon only two hydrogens.
Omitting C–H bonds in a displayed answer.
Calling the sketch a realistic bond-angle model.

diagram.alt: Original displayed formulas showing every bond in methane, ethane, propane, butane and pentane, with four bond contributions at each carbon.
diagram.caption: Expand all C–H bonds for a displayed answer. These are schematic connections, not the actual molecular angles.

practice.question: On paper draw the structural and fully displayed formulas of methane, ethane, propane, butane and pentane. Name each, show every C–H/C–C bond, and give the molecular formula sequence. Explain why CH₃CH₃ alone is not fully displayed.
practice.answer: The structural sequence is CH₄; CH₃CH₃; CH₃CH₂CH₃; CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃; CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. Molecular formulas are CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈, C₄H₁₀, C₅H₁₂, with names methane through pentane. Draw four individual C–H bonds for methane; in each longer chain draw all single C–C bonds, three H on each terminal carbon and two on each internal carbon. Compare with the original drawing sheet: every carbon must have four bond contributions. CH₃ groups abbreviate bonds and are structural notation, not a fully displayed answer.
practice.explanation: Check labels, individual bonds and atom totals on the actual drawing, rather than only recalling a general formula. The flat layout shows connectivity rather than real molecular angles.

sections.title: Check the three acyclic C₅H₁₂ skeletons
paragraphs: For C₅H₁₂, the three distinct acyclic alkane skeletons are the unbranched five-carbon chain, a four-carbon chain with one methyl branch, and a three-carbon chain with two methyl branches at its middle carbon. Their condensed formulas are CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ and C(CH₃)₄.

The last central carbon has four carbon-carbon single bonds and no hydrogen. Its four surrounding CH₃ groups supply all twelve hydrogens. In the one-branch isomer, the branch-bearing CH has one hydrogen, not two.

The corresponding systematic names help distinguish the skeletons, but the specific alkane naming requirement names the unbranched-chain isomers. These extra branch labels support the general naming and structural-isomer explanation; no exhaustive six-carbon isomer bank is claimed.

example.question: Why must the central carbon in C(CH₃)₄ have no hydrogen?
steps: It already has four C–C single bonds.
A further C–H bond would give five bond contributions.
The surrounding four CH₃ groups already give C₅H₁₂.
example.explanation: Normal carbon valency constrains the atom count.

commonMistakes: Adding a hydrogen to a carbon already bonded four times.
Counting a rotated branched skeleton as another isomer.

diagram.alt: Original full displayed formulas for 2-methylpropane C4H10, 2-methylbutane C5H12 and 2,2-dimethylpropane C5H12. Branch-bearing hydrogen counts satisfy carbon valency.
diagram.caption: Branch names support the general isomer explanation. The specific alkane naming reference asks for the unbranched names.

practice.question: Draw the structural and fully displayed formulas for all three acyclic C₅H₁₂ skeletons. Explain the hydrogen count on the branch carbon in CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ and on the central carbon in C(CH₃)₄. Is rotating either a fourth skeleton?
practice.answer: The three skeletons are CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ and C(CH₃)₄. Expand every H and single bond, comparing with the straight-chain and branched drawing sheets. The one-branch CH has three C neighbours and one H; the central C in C(CH₃)₄ has four C neighbours and no H. Totals are C₅H₁₂ for each. Rotations preserve the same connections and create no fourth skeleton.
practice.explanation: The unbranched name pentane is required in the specific naming set. The branch labels 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane help discuss connections; no exhaustive six-carbon isomer collection is asserted.

sections.title: Replace one alkane hydrogen under ultraviolet radiation
paragraphs: In the specified alkane-halogen reaction, ultraviolet radiation enables substitution of one hydrogen by a halogen atom. For methane and chlorine, the mono-substitution model is CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, with UV shown as a condition rather than a chemical reactant.

One chlorine atom takes the replaced hydrogen’s position and the other forms hydrogen chloride. The organic product is chloromethane, which contains chlorine and is no longer a hydrocarbon. The school scope is mono-substitution; additional substitution can occur under other circumstances and is not treated as impossible.

For larger alkanes, replacing hydrogens at different nonequivalent positions can give different mono-substitution products. Do not assume an unsymmetrical alkane necessarily makes only one constitutional product. No reaction mechanism or unsupervised halogen/UV procedure is required here.

example.question: Balance the methane/bromine mono-substitution model and name the required radiation condition.
steps: CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr.
The atoms balance: C₁H₄Br₂ on both sides.
Ultraviolet radiation is the specified condition.
example.explanation: Substitution replaces a hydrogen and forms a hydrogen halide.

commonMistakes: Writing only CH₃Br and losing the replaced hydrogen.
Drawing addition across a nonexistent alkane double bond.
Treating UV as a consumed chemical.

practice.question: Write a balanced mono-substitution model for ethane and chlorine under the required condition. Give the organic product’s structural formula and explain where both Cl atoms go. Does this mean further substitution is impossible?
practice.answer: CH₃CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃CH₂Cl + HCl, with ultraviolet radiation as a condition. One Cl replaces one H in chloroethane; the other combines with that H in HCl. Both sides contain C₂H₆Cl₂. The task is limited to mono-substitution, not a claim that further substitution cannot occur.
practice.explanation: UV is not a consumed chemical reactant. Ethane’s equivalent hydrogen positions give one mono-substitution connectivity here; an unsymmetrical larger alkane can have several position products. No mechanism is required.

sections.title: Identify a C=C group and the alkene formula
paragraphs: The named alkene functional group is a carbon-carbon double bond, C=C. Acyclic hydrocarbons with one such double bond have general formula CₙH₂ₙ. The first member is ethene C₂H₄; a one-carbon molecule cannot have a carbon-carbon double bond.

Alkenes are unsaturated because the multiple bond permits addition, such as adding bromine across the C=C. The two carbon atoms remain connected after simple addition, but by a single bond; the extra bond contributions connect the added atoms.

The formula CₙH₂ₙ alone does not uniquely prove an alkene because other structures can have that atom ratio. Use a displayed structure or the stated family. The required drawing range has one C=C and up to four carbons, without compulsory E/Z or cis/trans notation.

example.question: An acyclic one-double-bond alkene has three carbons. What formula is expected?
steps: n = 3 in CₙH₂ₙ.
The formula is C₃H₆.
The structure must still place the C=C bond and satisfy carbon valency.
example.explanation: Use the family’s stated structural conditions.

commonMistakes: Giving ethene C₂H₆.
Proposing a one-carbon alkene.
Treating a molecular ratio as proof of a double bond.

practice.question: For an acyclic hydrocarbon with one C=C and five carbons, give the general and molecular formulas and explain unsaturation. Why is C₅H₁₀ alone insufficient evidence of C=C? Could a one-carbon molecule be an alkene?
practice.answer: General formula CₙH₂ₙ gives C₅H₁₀. Its C=C functional group permits addition and makes it unsaturated. That atom ratio alone does not exclude a ring structure, so the stated family or actual structure is needed. One carbon cannot form a carbon–carbon double bond; ethene is the first member.
practice.explanation: General-formula application is distinct from the smaller required alkene drawing set. In simple addition the original two carbons remain connected, but their bond becomes single.

sections.title: Draw and distinguish the required small alkenes
paragraphs: The unbranched examples up to four carbons are ethene CH₂=CH₂, propene CH₂=CHCH₃, but-1-ene CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ and but-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃. For four carbons the two unbranched double-bond positions are distinct structural isomers, while writing but-1-ene from the opposite end does not add another.

The branched four-carbon alkene CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ provides another valid connectivity for the drawing requirement; its double-bonded branch carbon has no hydrogen. The specific naming requirement covers the unbranched isomers. Cis/trans or E/Z descriptors are not required in this course reference.

In displayed formulas, show both C=C lines and all C–H bonds. A double bond contributes two to each connected carbon’s valency. The schematic arrangements show connectivity only; orientation on the sheet is not a claim of a particular stereoisomer.

example.question: Draw fully displayed but-2-ene and determine each double-bond carbon’s hydrogens.
steps: Draw CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃, showing both double-bond lines and expanding every H/bond rather than leaving condensed groups.
Each double-bond carbon has one single bond to a CH₃ group and the double bond to the other carbon.
That gives three bond contributions before adding H.
Each needs one H; total formula is C₄H₈.
example.explanation: Count bond contributions, not just the number of neighbouring labels.

commonMistakes: Drawing three H on a carbon already in C=C.
Counting opposite drawing directions as different positions.
Requiring E/Z names beyond the stated scope.

diagram.alt: Original fully displayed ethene, propene, but-1-ene, but-2-ene and the branched C4 alkene. Double bonds and every hydrogen are drawn without stereochemical assignments.
diagram.caption: Different double-bond positions can change connectivity. Drawing orientation does not create a new isomer; stereochemical descriptors are not required.

practice.question: Draw structural and fully displayed formulas for ethene, propene, both unbranched C₄H₈ alkenes, and the branched acyclic C₄H₈ alkene. Name the unbranched structures and check the branch carbon’s H count. Are cis/trans or E/Z labels required?
practice.answer: Ethene CH₂=CH₂; propene CH₂=CHCH₃; but-1-ene CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃; but-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃; branched CH₂=C(CH₃)₂. Expand all C–H bonds and both C=C lines as on the original drawing sheet. In the branched structure, the substituted double-bond carbon has two C–C single bonds plus the double bond and no H. Molecular totals are C₂H₄, C₃H₆, then C₄H₈ for the last three. No cis/trans or E/Z notation is required.
practice.explanation: Check connectivity and four bond contributions per carbon. Reversing but-1-ene does not add a different unbranched double-bond position; the stated naming set asks for unbranched names.

sections.title: Add bromine across the alkene double bond
paragraphs: In the required simple model, Br₂ adds across the C=C of an alkene to form a dibromoalkane. For ethene: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. Each former double-bond carbon gains one bromine, and the carbon-carbon bond is now single.

The product is 1,2-dibromoethane, not bromoethene or a substitution product with HBr removed. The model conserves C₂H₄Br₂ on both sides. For propene the bromines attach at the two original double-bond carbons, giving CH₂BrCHBrCH₃.

This is the syllabus’s dibromoalkane addition model. An actual aqueous reagent can involve additional chemistry; the colour test identifies the specified unsaturation response rather than certifying a pure isolated dibromo product. Mechanisms are not required.

example.question: Write the structural product of bromine addition to CH₃CH=CHCH₃ in the required model.
steps: Change the C=C to C–C.
Add Br to each of those two carbons.
The product is CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃, with no hydrogen removed.
example.explanation: Preserve the skeleton and add across the two-carbon group.

commonMistakes: Putting both Br atoms on one carbon for this addition model.
Keeping the C=C while adding too many bonds.
Creating HBr as though a hydrogen were substituted.

practice.question: Draw structural and fully displayed products when Br₂ adds to CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ in the required model. Show where each Br attaches, recount atoms and decide whether HBr is a product.
practice.answer: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCHBrCH₂CH₃. Change the original C=C to one C–C bond; attach one Br to each of those two carbons. In the full drawing, the terminal former double-bond carbon has two H and one Br; the other has one H and one Br, in addition to its C neighbours. Both sides contain C₄H₈Br₂. No H is replaced and no HBr is produced in this addition model.
practice.explanation: Keep the carbon skeleton and all original hydrogens. Putting both Br on one carbon while retaining the same H counts would not represent this required across-double-bond addition.

sections.title: Use a controlled bromine-water colour comparison
paragraphs: In the supervised comparison, add bromine water to the sample and mix as directed. An alkene removes the bromine colour: orange or orange-brown becomes colourless under suitable conditions. An alkane does not show that prompt reaction in the comparison without UV; avoid UV or strong sunlight that can permit substitution.

Name the original reagent colour and its disappearance rather than saying “the alkene turns clear”. Some samples form two layers; distinguish a reaction removing bromine from its physical transfer between layers, and keep reagent amounts and mixing comparable. Excess bromine can leave colour even when some alkene reacted.

The test distinguishes the specified alkane/alkene candidates in the task context. Other reactive substances can also decolourise bromine, so a positive response in an unrestricted unknown does not uniquely identify one compound or certify purity. Bromine is hazardous; use the teacher-approved dilute reagent and handling rather than direct inhalation or a home recipe.

example.question: Two stated hydrocarbon candidates are an alkane and an alkene. One promptly makes bromine water colourless under matched conditions without UV. What does that support?
steps: The responding sample is the alkene in this specified comparison.
Bromine reacts with its C=C group.
The observation does not name the exact alkene or certify purity.
example.explanation: Connect the observation to the restricted candidate set.

commonMistakes: Treating physical movement of colour between layers as proof of reaction.
Using UV during the distinction and ignoring alkane substitution.
Claiming every decolourising unknown must be one pure alkene.

practice.question: Two specified candidates are hexane and an alkene. Under matched mixing/reagent conditions without UV, A promptly changes bromine water from orange-brown to colourless; B retains the colour. Identify the supported candidate for each. Explain a two-layer, excess-reagent or unrestricted-unknown limitation.
practice.answer: A supports the alkene and B hexane in this restricted comparison. Avoid UV/strong sunlight that could allow alkane substitution. Bromine moving into another liquid layer is not the same as chemical removal of its colour; excess reagent may remain coloured despite some addition. An unrestricted unknown can contain other bromine-reactive substances, so decolourisation alone does not identify a unique pure alkene.
practice.explanation: State the starting reagent colour and its disappearance, not merely that the sample looks clear. Use the approved dilute reagent and supervised comparison; this is a proposed interpretation, not an experiment performed here.

sections.title: Recognize the alcohol group — Paper 2C
paragraphs: The required alcohol functional group is –OH bonded to the organic carbon framework. Methanol CH₃OH and ethanol CH₃CH₂OH are examples. The oxygen has two bonds: one to carbon and one to hydrogen. The –OH here is a covalent group, not a free hydroxide ion.

Do not classify a carboxylic acid as an alcohol just because its –COOH includes O–H: the surrounding carbonyl connection makes a different functional group. Alcohols contain oxygen and are not hydrocarbons.

example.question: Why does ethanol not meet the hydrocarbon definition?
steps: Its formula includes an oxygen atom.
Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only.
Ethanol is an alcohol, although it is still an organic compound.
example.explanation: Check both composition and functional-group connections.

commonMistakes: Treating an alcohol’s OH as OH⁻ in solution.
Calling every organic O–H an alcohol.

practice.question: Compare CH₃CH₂OH, CH₃COOH and aqueous OH⁻. Which contains the alcohol functional group, which contains a carboxyl group, and which is an ion? Give the oxygen bonding and hydrocarbon classification for ethanol.
practice.answer: CH₃CH₂OH is an alcohol: its oxygen makes single bonds to the carbon framework and H. CH₃COOH has the complete C(=O)–OH carboxyl group, not an isolated alcohol group. OH⁻ is hydroxide, an ion, rather than the covalent –OH connection in ethanol. Ethanol contains oxygen and is not a hydrocarbon.
practice.explanation: Read connections around the O–H, not just the letters OH. Normal neutral alcohol oxygen has two bonds.

sections.title: Draw and name the four required alcohols — Paper 2C
paragraphs: The required structures are methanol CH₃OH, ethanol CH₃CH₂OH, propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH and butan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH. Propanol and butanol are accepted in the own specification for these named primary structures; giving the position as 1 makes the connection explicit.

The alcohol carbon-count root includes every carbon in the chain, and -ol identifies the alcohol group. In a displayed drawing, expand all carbon-hydrogen bonds and show the C–O–H connections. A terminal carbon attached to oxygen has two hydrogen atoms if it is also attached to another carbon.

The explicit 4.30C set has the OH at carbon 1 for the three- and four-carbon examples. Do not silently substitute propan-2-ol when the task asks for the named primary structure. The original diagrams show connections, not real molecular angles.

example.question: Draw structural and fully displayed butan-1-ol and count its atoms.
steps: Draw four connected carbons with single bonds and C–O–H at the terminal carbon. Expand H counts3,2,2,2 on the carbons and one on oxygen; use the original displayed sheet to check every bond.
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH.
There are four carbons, ten hydrogens including the O–H hydrogen, and one oxygen.
Its molecular formula is C₄H₁₀O.
example.explanation: Count the hydrogen on oxygen as well as those on carbon.

commonMistakes: Giving the OH-bearing CH₂ three hydrogens as well as both C and O bonds.
Replacing propan-1-ol with propan-2-ol in the named set.

diagram.alt: Full displayed formulas of methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol, showing every hydrogen including the one on oxygen.
diagram.caption: Four named primary structures. Position 1 is explicit for propanol and butanol; schematic geometry.

practice.question: Draw and name structural and fully displayed formulas for the four specified alcohols. Give each molecular formula and distinguish the required three-carbon structure from propan-2-ol.
practice.answer: Methanol CH₃OH (CH₄O); ethanol CH₃CH₂OH (C₂H₆O); propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (C₃H₈O); butan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (C₄H₁₀O). Expand every C–H, C–O and O–H bond as on the original drawing sheet. In the three-/four-carbon required structures the OH-bearing terminal carbon is CH₂, not the middle CH(OH) of propan-2-ol. Count the O–H hydrogen.
practice.explanation: The source accepts propanol and butanol for its specified primary structures; using -1-ol makes the position explicit. All four carbons/oxygens must satisfy their normal valencies.

sections.title: Distinguish ethanol combustion from acid formation — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Complete combustion of ethanol with oxygen forms carbon dioxide and water: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. Ethanol already contains one oxygen, so include it when balancing the added oxygen requirement.

The products of complete combustion are not ethanoic acid. Producing ethanoic acid by microbial oxidation or a chemical oxidant retains the two-carbon framework in the acid. All are oxidation routes in the required list, but their conditions and products differ.

example.question: Check the oxygen balance in complete ethanol combustion.
steps: The left has one oxygen in ethanol and six in three O₂ molecules, total seven.
The right has four in two CO₂ and three in three H₂O, total seven.
The equation balances without changing ethanol’s formula.
example.explanation: Count oxygen already in the organic reactant.

commonMistakes: Using the hydrocarbon-only oxygen count for an alcohol.
Giving ethanoic acid as the complete-combustion product.

practice.question: Balance complete combustion of two ethanol molecules with whole-number coefficients. Check all element totals, and contrast the organic carbon destination with controlled oxidation to ethanoic acid.
practice.answer: 2C₂H₅OH + 6O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Both sides have C₄H₁₂O₁₄; include the two oxygens already present in the two alcohol molecules. Complete combustion puts the carbon into CO₂, whereas controlled acid-forming oxidation retains the two-carbon framework in each ethanoic acid molecule.
practice.explanation: These routes have different products and conditions even though the specified reactions are oxidation routes. Do not use a hydrocarbon-only oxygen count for an alcohol.

sections.title: Use the two specified routes to ethanoic acid — Paper 2C
paragraphs: The own specification gives microbial oxidation using oxygen in air, and heating with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid, as routes from ethanol to ethanoic acid. The microbial route requires suitable microorganisms and oxygen; it is different from anaerobic glucose fermentation that makes ethanol.

A balanced oxygen model is C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O. For the chemical-oxidant shorthand, CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O uses [O] to represent oxidising equivalents, not a measured bottle of monatomic oxygen.

Controlled heating with sufficient oxidant can take oxidation through to the acid; partial oxidation can form a different intermediate and should not be confused with the required final product. Dichromate(VI) and acid require approved laboratory handling and waste collection; a nearby demonstration’s drain-disposal suggestion is not adopted here.

example.question: What key condition distinguishes microbial oxidation of ethanol to acid from fermentation of glucose to ethanol?
steps: The microbial acid-forming route uses oxygen from air.
The specified ethanol fermentation is carried out without air.
They start from different substances and produce different organic products.
example.explanation: Conditions belong to the named route, not to every microbial process.

commonMistakes: Saying the acid-forming route is the same as glucose fermentation.
Substituting a different oxidant for the named course reagent.
Interpreting [O] as a literal gas formula.

practice.question: Plan on paper two specified routes that turn ethanol into ethanoic acid: identify the biological oxygen condition and the named chemical reagent/acid/heating condition. Give balanced oxygen and [O] models and distinguish both from glucose fermentation.
practice.answer: Microbial oxidation uses suitable microorganisms and oxygen from air: C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O. The chemical route heats ethanol with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid, with conditions/sufficient oxidant that give the acid endpoint: CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O. [O] represents oxidising equivalents. Anaerobic glucose fermentation instead makes ethanol and CO₂.
practice.explanation: Do not swap the named oxidant or confuse dilute sulfuric acid here with the concentrated catalyst example for ester preparation. No actual dichromate experiment or disposal has been performed.

sections.title: Manufacture ethanol from ethene and steam — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Ethene reacts with steam to form ethanol: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH in the simplified formation equation. The required conditions are a phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300°C and about 60–70 atm. Keep these together; they are not the fermentation conditions.

Water’s elements add across the double bond in this hydration route. The ethene carbon skeleton is retained and the product has an alcohol group. This is an industrial process, not a school method using a sealed flask at the stated pressure.

A catalyst increases the reaction rate rather than being written as a consumed reactant. This lesson gives the specified route and conditions, not an independently optimized factory yield or a claim that every molecule converts in one pass.

example.question: Which catalyst and temperature belong to ethene hydration rather than glucose fermentation?
steps: Phosphoric acid is the named catalyst.
The temperature is about 300°C, with about 60–70 atm pressure.
Yeast enzymes and about 30°C belong to fermentation instead.
example.explanation: Avoid mixing the two manufacturing routes.

commonMistakes: Using sulfuric acid as the named industrial catalyst.
Giving fermentation’s temperature for steam hydration.

practice.question: Correct a route card that says “ethene + steam → ethanol; yeast catalyst, 30 °C, atmospheric pressure”. Give the balanced formation equation, all specified industrial conditions and why the catalyst is not a consumed reactant.
practice.answer: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH in the simplified formation equation. Use phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C and about 60–70 atm. Yeast enzymes and about 30 °C belong to fermentation. A catalyst provides a faster pathway and is chemically unchanged overall, so it is written as a condition rather than consumed in this overall equation.
practice.explanation: This is the specified industrial route, not an instruction to pressurise a school flask or a claim of complete one-pass conversion.

sections.title: Manufacture ethanol from glucose — Paper 2C
paragraphs: The specified fermentation uses glucose, enzymes in yeast, absence of air and an optimum temperature of about 30°C. The overall model is C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. It conserves C₆, H₁₂ and O₆.

The reaction produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, so a gas outlet is needed in a safe supervised setup. “Without air” does not mean sealing an actively gas-producing flask with no way to release pressure. The resulting liquid is a mixture containing water and other material rather than automatically pure ethanol.

The word equation and conditions describe manufacture. Separation and purification are later physical steps if a task asks for a concentrated or pure product. No fermentation has actually been carried out here.

example.question: In the fermentation model, how many moles of ethanol correspond to one mole of glucose converted?
steps: The coefficient ratio is one glucose to two ethanol.
One mole of converted glucose gives two moles of ethanol in the ideal equation.
Real yield can differ, so the ratio is not proof of an achieved practical yield.
example.explanation: Read the stoichiometric model separately from measured production.

commonMistakes: Writing oxygen as a required reactant in this route.
Calling the fermentation mixture pure ethanol.
Blocking the CO₂ outlet.

practice.question: Write the glucose fermentation equation and word products, state the required biological/air/temperature conditions, and calculate the ideal ethanol amount from 0.300 mol glucose converted. Is the collected liquid necessarily pure ethanol?
practice.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂: glucose forms ethanol and carbon dioxide. Use enzymes in yeast, absence of air and an optimum of about 30 °C. The ideal ratio gives 0.600 mol ethanol from 0.300 mol glucose converted; actual yield needs measurement. The liquid remains a mixture containing water and other substances, not automatically pure ethanol.
practice.explanation: Air exclusion is compatible with a suitable CO₂ outlet; it does not justify blocking a gas-producing vessel. The balanced equation conserves C₆H₁₂O₆.

sections.title: Explain the absence of air and temperature choice — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Absence of air supports the anaerobic route that produces ethanol rather than oxygen-supported respiration. If oxygen is available, yeast can use a different respiratory route, and suitable microbes can oxidise ethanol further. Do not say all yeast activity requires oxygen or that every microbial reaction is anaerobic.

At low temperatures enzyme-controlled fermentation is slower. An appropriate optimum near the course’s stated 30°C balances activity with the enzymes’ stability; excessive temperature can denature the enzymes and reduce or stop useful fermentation. The optimum is not a universal identical value for every yeast strain and condition.

Explain these choices using the product wanted and the enzyme-controlled process. Raising temperature cannot indefinitely increase an enzyme reaction’s rate, and boiling to make a reaction faster defeats the intended living-yeast process.

example.question: Why is “use the highest possible temperature to make more ethanol quickly” unsuitable?
steps: Fermentation depends on yeast enzymes.
Excessive heating can denature them.
Use the specified suitable optimum, not unlimited heating.
example.explanation: An enzyme rate trend has a high-temperature limit.

commonMistakes: Saying enzymes are killed while ignoring denaturation as the explanation.
Confusing absence of air with an unsafe blocked gas outlet.

practice.question: Explain two faults in an invented ethanol-fermentation plan: continuous air supply and “the hotter the better”. State the course conditions and why air exclusion must not mean a rigidly sealed gas outlet.
practice.answer: The intended ethanol route is anaerobic; air permits oxygen-supported pathways instead of maintaining the intended conditions. Use the specified optimum near 30 °C: low temperature slows enzyme activity, while excessive heat can denature enzymes rather than continually increase useful rate. Fermentation generates CO₂, so use approved air-excluding apparatus that still permits gas release, not a blocked rigid vessel.
practice.explanation: Conditions depend on the desired product and enzyme-controlled process. Microbial oxidation of ethanol to acid uses oxygen and is a different route.

sections.title: Recognize the complete carboxyl group — Paper 2C
paragraphs: A carboxylic acid has the –C(=O)–OH group, often condensed to –COOH. The same carbon is double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to the OH oxygen. Recognize both parts as one group rather than treating it as an isolated alcohol OH.

The carboxyl carbon counts in the molecule’s carbon total and in the chain name. In methanoic acid it is bonded to hydrogen; in ethanoic acid it is bonded to CH₃. Normal valencies require four bond contributions at this carbon and two at each oxygen.

example.question: How many carbon atoms are in CH₃COOH?
steps: There is one carbon in CH₃ and one in COOH.
The total is two.
The compound is ethanoic acid, not a one-carbon acid.
example.explanation: Do not omit the carbon in the functional group.

commonMistakes: Drawing C–O–O–H without the required carbonyl.
Counting only the hydrocarbon fragment.

practice.question: Draw the complete functional group in CH₃CH₂COOH with its bonds to both oxygens. Count all carbons and explain why C–O–O–H or a free hydroxide ion would not be the same group.
practice.answer: Draw CH₃CH₂–C(=O)–O–H. The carbonyl carbon counts as the third carbon, so this is propanoic acid. It has a double bond to one O, a single bond to the OH oxygen and a single bond to the carbon chain. Each O has two bond contributions. C–O–O–H omits the carbonyl connection; free OH⁻ is an ion, not this covalent carboxyl group.
practice.explanation: Treat –C(=O)–OH as one functional group and include its carbon in the chain name.

sections.title: Draw the first four unbranched acids — Paper 2C
paragraphs: The required unbranched structures are methanoic acid HCOOH, ethanoic acid CH₃COOH, propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH and butanoic acid CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH. Their names count the carboxyl carbon: one, two, three and four respectively.

For displayed formulas, expand all C–H bonds and show the C=O and C–O–H bonds separately. The carboxyl carbon already uses three bond contributions for its two oxygen connections and has only one remaining bond to H or the rest of the chain.

The own required set ends at four carbons for these unbranched acid drawings. Do not replace an acid name with the corresponding alcohol’s -ol suffix. The drawing sheet shows connections rather than realistic bond geometry.

example.question: Draw structural and fully displayed propanoic acid and count its carbons.
steps: Draw CH₃–CH₂–C(=O)–O–H, expand the five C-bound H atoms and keep the O–H bond and carbonyl double bond.
CH₃CH₂COOH.
The CH₃ and CH₂ supply two carbons.
The COOH carbon makes three in total.
example.explanation: The acid group is part of the named chain.

commonMistakes: Drawing CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH and calling it propanoic acid.
Omitting the carbonyl double bond in a displayed acid.

diagram.alt: Full displayed methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acids. Each shows C=O and C–O–H with the carboxyl carbon included in the carbon total.
diagram.caption: Count the carboxyl carbon in the name and preserve the double bond to oxygen.

practice.question: Draw structural and fully displayed formulas and name all four required unbranched carboxylic acids. Give each molecular formula, expand all H bonds and show both oxygen connections.
practice.answer: Methanoic acid HCOOH (CH₂O₂); ethanoic acid CH₃COOH (C₂H₄O₂); propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH (C₃H₆O₂); butanoic acid CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (C₄H₈O₂). In each displayed drawing show C=O and C–O–H, with every C–H bond as on the drawing sheet. Methanoic acid has H directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon; in the other three that position bonds to the carbon chain. Count the COOH carbon and O–H hydrogen.
practice.explanation: The first four named structures are not the corresponding alcohols. Check four bond contributions at each C and two at each O; an acid formula without C=O is not a correct displayed answer.

sections.title: Form a carboxylate salt and hydrogen with a suitable metal — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Aqueous carboxylic acids can react with a suitable metal above hydrogen in the relevant reactivity context to form a salt and hydrogen. For ethanoic acid and magnesium: 2CH₃COOH + Mg → Mg(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂.
The carboxylate ion in the salt is CH₃COO⁻ for ethanoate. Magnesium is Mg²⁺, so two ethanoate ions are needed. The acidic O–H hydrogens are involved; the CH₃ groups remain in this simple reaction.

Do not assume every metal reacts under the same conditions. The gas test for hydrogen is a lighted splint pop in the supervised method. A weak acid may react more slowly than a matched strong acid; weak does not mean unable to react.

example.question: Why is the magnesium salt Mg(CH₃COO)₂ rather than MgCH₃COO?
steps: Magnesium ions have charge +2.
Each ethanoate ion has charge −1.
Two ethanoate ions balance one magnesium ion.
example.explanation: Salt charge and atom counts both need checking.

commonMistakes: Giving oxygen gas instead of hydrogen.
Keeping the acid’s O–H in each carboxylate ion.
Assuming copper behaves like magnesium in dilute acid.

practice.question: For dilute aqueous propanoic acid reacting with magnesium, write word and balanced formula equations for the salt and gas. Explain the salt’s two carboxylate groups and name the gas test. Would the same observation automatically follow for copper?
practice.answer: Propanoic acid + magnesium → magnesium propanoate + hydrogen. 2CH₃CH₂COOH + Mg → Mg(CH₃CH₂COO)₂ + H₂. Mg²⁺ needs two singly negative propanoate ions. Both sides have C₆H₁₂O₄Mg; hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint in the supervised test. Copper is below hydrogen in the relevant simple acid-reactivity context, so the magnesium result cannot automatically be transferred to copper.
practice.explanation: The acidic O–H hydrogen is removed in each carboxylate; the organic carbon framework is retained. Weak acid does not mean no possible metal reaction.

sections.title: Identify salt, water and carbon dioxide — Paper 2C
